hook: The father of Impressionism, who painted light, haystacks and his water lily pond.

pages.x: Claude Monet was born in Paris in 1840 and grew up in the port of Le Havre. As a teenager he sold funny drawings of local people. The painter Eugène Boudin taught him to paint outdoors, in the open air.
In 1872 he painted the harbour of Le Havre in the morning mist, quickly and loosely. When it was shown, a critic mocked its title and called Monet and his friends "Impressionists". The name stuck.
For years Monet and his wife Camille were so poor that he begged friends for money, and creditors seized his paintings. Camille, who posed for many of his pictures, died in 1879.
pages.img: Woman with a Parasol – Madame Monet and Her Son

pages.x: He painted the same haystacks, and later the front of Rouen Cathedral, again and again, at different hours and seasons. He worked on many canvases at once, switching as the light changed.
In 1883 he moved to Giverny, and made a garden with a pond full of water lilies and a Japanese bridge. He even changed the course of a stream to fill it. "My garden is my most beautiful masterpiece."
pages.img: Bridge over a Pond of Water Lilies

pages.x: He loved London fog. From his room at the Savoy hotel he painted the Thames and the Houses of Parliament dozens of times. Without fog, he said, London would not be a beautiful city.
In his last 30 years he painted his pond about 250 times. Even when cataracts clouded his eyes, he worked on giant water lily murals, which now fill two oval rooms in Paris.
Monet led the Impressionists, who freed painting from strict rules and led the way to modern art.
